The researchers note that, in the future, this system could be adapted to slow cellular aging and enhance cancer therapies. Additionally, the finding offers insight into an ancient evolutionary event that may have set the stage for the emergence of higher organisms.

content:

Creating these tailored fields currently requires researchers and engineers to design specialized, carefully optimized magnets or large systems of coils for each individual application. This process is complex and resource-intensive.
summary: Magnetic fields are invisible yet essential components in technologies ranging from MRI scanners and particle accelerators to atomic clocks and future quantum computers. Each of these applications requires magnetic fields with specific shapes and properties.

content:

The discovery came after centuries of mining had erased much of the archaeological record, allowing researchers to trace the industry’s origins.  

The findings were published in the journal Antiquity.

content:
Recent research has revealed a deep connection between gravity and quantum information, showing that the shape of spacetime can be traced back to the way information is stored in quantum fields. The study derives Einstein’s equations from principles of quantum information, suggesting that gravitational dynamics may emerge from underlying informational structures.

The work indicates that the geometry of spacetime is not an independent backdrop but is determined by the distribution and storage of quantum information within fields. This finding links the fundamental laws of gravity to the informational content of quantum systems.

Snake envenoming is a potentially fatal condition that mainly affects poor rural communities in tropical and subtropical regions where access to medical care is limited.

title: Chatham House analyst says Moscow is playing with Washington over diesel export deal
content:
President Donald Trump’s envoys told Ukrainian officials on Friday that a proposed deal to permit Russian diesel exports is intended to coax Russia back into negotiations after earlier attempts to launch sustained talks to end the war failed, three people familiar with the meeting said, according to Reuters.  

In a separate interview, FRANCE 24’s Sharon Gaffney spoke with Grégoire Roos, director of the Europe and Russia and Eurasia Programmes at Chatham House. Roos said, “It’s clear that Moscow is just playing with Washington because Vladimir Putin knows that Donald Trump lives on borrowed time.”  

Both remarks highlight ongoing diplomatic efforts and differing assessments of Moscow’s strategy toward the United States.
summary: President Donald Trump's envoys told Ukrainian officials that a deal to allow Russian diesel exports is meant to draw Russia back to negotiations after earlier attempts failed. content:

During the raid, police shot dead Eduardo Rózsa Flores, a Bolivian‑Croatian, Michael Dwyer, an Irishman, and Árpád Magyarosi, a Hungarian‑Romanian. The investigation also alleges that two other European individuals were tortured in connection with the same incident.

title: NASA Seeks Ideas to Prevent Static Electricity from Zapping Astronauts on Moon Missions
content: NASA has issued a request for proposals seeking solutions to prevent static electricity from damaging astronauts or critical hardware during lunar missions. The agency is looking for innovative ideas to address the potential hazards posed by electrostatic discharge in the moon’s environment.
summary: The moon could turn astronauts into walking, high‑voltage capacitors that accidentally zap spacecraft. NASA is asking for ideas to stop static electricity from zapping astronauts or critical hardware during moon missions.
author: Space.com

title: Julie Hesmondhalgh leaves Celebrity Traitors with head held high
content:
Julie Hesmondhalgh, a former Coronation Street star, stated that she left the Celebrity Traitors show "with head held high." The comment followed her banishment during the episode aired on Friday.

Hesmondhalgh disclosed that she received several apologetic text messages from other participants after her elimination.
summary: Julie Hesmondhalgh left Celebrity Traitors with head held high after being banished on Friday's episode. She received apologetic texts following her exit.

title: Hepworth sculpture inspired by Cornish landscape could fetch £8m at auction
content:
Hepworth piece could fetch up to £8m at auction

A post‑war sculpture by the late artist Barbara Hepworth, inspired by the Cornish landscape, is set to go under the hammer. The work could fetch up to £8 million at auction, according to the latest reports.
summary: A post‑war sculpture inspired by the Cornish landscape is set to go under the hammer. The piece could fetch up to £8m at auction.

title: Balding and O'Brien contest trainers' title at Ascot Champions Day
content:
Champions Day at Ascot on Saturday offers a potential finale to the British Flat season, featuring five Group One races and a £250,000 juvenile event. The card includes a live contest for the UK Flat trainers’ championship, pitting Andrew Balding against Aidan O’Brien in a head-to-head battle that adds significant interest to the day’s proceedings.

The trainer’s title race has seen a shift in odds, with Balding starting the week as a 6-4 shot with Paddy Power after previously being a double-figure price. O’Brien, aiming for his third consecutive title and ninth overall, is the favorite at 1-2. Both trainers have already surpassed John Gosden’s record prize-money total of £8.52m from 2017, highlighting their dominance of the campaign ahead of the final day.
summary: Andrew Balding and Aidan O'Brien will battle for the UK Flat trainers' championship during the five Group One races at Ascot. Both trainers have already surpassed John Gosden's 2017 record prize-money total of £8.52m before the event.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Manchester City’s 3-0 win over Liverpool fails to lift crisis, says Wilson
content:
Erling Haaland’s comments regarding Manchester City’s 3-0 victory over Liverpool on Sunday have drawn attention to the unusual language used to describe the club’s recent financial charges. Football writer Jonathan Wilson argues that the situation is not merely about the unprecedented nature of the charges, but specifically about the terminology employed to discuss them. Wilson notes that while footballers typically speak a nuanced dialect of the game, applying this specific argot to other subjects can sound jarring.

Haaland, described as a bright and engaging player with a quirky self-awareness, made an assessment of the win that highlighted these linguistic tensions. Wilson suggests that minor deviations from familiar football language can signal underlying issues, prompting questions about what is truly happening and what players are hinting at. The article posits that for Manchester City, winning the match was not sufficient to move past the current crisis, as the manner in which the club’s situation is discussed remains a central point of contention.
summary: Erling Haaland is described as a bright and engaging player who steps outside norms. Wilson notes that Manchester City’s 3‑0 victory over Liverpool on Sunday does not resolve the club’s crisis.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Independent Football Regulator to recommend cost controls as 94% of clubs lose money
content:
The Independent Football Regulator (IFR) plans to recommend that clubs implement greater cost controls in its long-awaited State of the Game report, scheduled for publication on Tuesday. The 250-page draft report presents a critical assessment of the financial state of English men’s football, highlighting that 94% of the top 116 clubs are currently operating at a loss.

The document includes recommendations aimed at improving the sustainability of the sport. A final version of the report is expected to be released in the spring, following an eight-week public consultation period that begins this week.
summary: The Independent Football Regulator (IFR) will recommend that clubs introduce greater cost controls in its State of the Game report. The 250‑page draft report, released on Tuesday, finds that 94% of the top 116 English men’s football clubs are loss‑making and will be followed by an eight‑week public consultation before a final version is published in the spring.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Renshaw's 190 in Durban pushes Australia toward first-Test victory
content:
Matt Renshaw’s return to the Australian Test side was marked by a dramatic performance in the first Test against South Africa in Durban. After a brief comeback innings of eight runs, he travelled to South Africa where his role as opener shifted to batting fifth.

Over the first two days of the match Renshaw scored an impressive 190, helping to rescue Australia from a precarious position. On the fourth day he added another 82, top‑scoring again as Australia declared at 316 for six. The Australians set South Africa 421 runs to win.

Australia’s bowlers closed the game with four wickets for 102, leaving South Africa reeling. Aiden Markram, who has scored 45, is expected to be the main obstacle to an Australian series lead on the final day.
summary: Matt Renshaw scored 190 in the first two days of the first Test in Durban and top scored again with 82 on the fourth day. Australia set South Africa 421 to win and took four wickets for 102 by the close, with Aiden Markram on 45 as the main obstacle to an Australian series lead.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Saracens sack academy player Totoa Auvaa after weekend incident
content:
Saracens have released academy player Totoa Auvaa following a recent incident. In a statement, the north London club said, “Prem club release statement after releasing Totoa Auvaa‘His conduct falls short of the standards expected’.”

Auvaa had earlier sparked the Ben Stokes captaincy crisis by throwing a punch at his England teammate Gus Atkinson. The club added that, “Following an incident this weekend, the club has determined that his conduct falls short of the standards expected of everyone who represents Saracens, both on and off the pitch,” read a statement fron the north London club.

The club indicated that more details would be provided soon.
summary: Saracens released a statement saying Totoa Auvaa's conduct falls short of the standards expected of everyone who represents Saracens, both on and off the pitch. The club has sacked the academy player, who previously sparked a Ben Stokes captaincy crisis by punching England teammate Gus Atkinson, after another incident over the weekend.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Matt Richardson dropped from GB cycling team amid claims of misconduct
content:
Matt Richardson has been withdrawn from the Great Britain squad for next week’s track world championships in Shanghai amid allegations of serious misconduct.  

The 27‑year‑old, who switched allegiances from Australia after the Paris 2024 Olympics, had been regarded as one of Britain’s strongest medal hopes, with chances in the team sprint, individual sprints and the keirin.  

Following a Times story that reported concerns about his behaviour from other riders, Richardson is now in the process of leaving the team’s training base in China.
summary: Rider was to take part in track world championshipsBritish Cycling confirms Richardson was withdrawnMatt Richardson has withdrawn from the Great Britain team for next week’s track world championships in Shanghai amid allegations of serious misconduct. The 27-year-old, who switched allegiances from Australia after the Paris 2024 Olympics, had been seen as one of Britain’s strongest medal hopes, with chances in the team and individual sprints and the keirin.

title: Christian Horner Reflects on Pain of Being Sacked After 20 Years at Red Bull
content:
Christian Horner, the 52‑year‑old team principal who led Red Bull Racing to become an F1 powerhouse over two decades, has spoken publicly about the pain he felt after being sacked. He described the experience as a source of panic attacks and has questioned his purpose in life following the abrupt end to his tenure.

The interview was conducted on an autumn morning in Highgate, where Horner was joined by his wife, Geri Halliwell‑Horner, a former Spice Girl. Halliwell‑Horner greeted the interviewer with a cheerful hug and performed an imitation of a South African accent, referencing her former headteacher at Watford Girls School.

During the conversation, the couple discussed their two daughters, who had attended Halliwell‑Horner’s school, and noted that one of the school’s history textbooks contained her name on an inside page. Halliwell‑Horner also spoke about the gritty nature of old Watford, grammar school education, and Nelson Mandela.
summary: Christian Horner, 52, reflects on the pain of being sacked after two decades turning Red Bull into an F1 powerhouse. He is questioning his purpose in life and dealing with panic attacks.
author: Guardian Sport

content:
Coventry City vs Newcastle United – Premier League live

The Premier League clash between Coventry City and Newcastle United is scheduled to kick off at 8 pm BST.  The live coverage will include ten talking points, a league table, and a top‑scorers list.

The decision came after Carlos Alcaraz suffered a surprise defeat in Shanghai, ensuring that Zverev will finish the season at the top of the ATP rankings.

content:

The question now is whether the Lionesses should push for a higher scoreline to secure a more comfortable cushion for the decisive encounter.

title: Obama releases ad supporting Scott Colom in Mississippi Senate race
content:
Former President Barack Obama released a new television advertisement this week in support of Democratic candidate Scott Colom in Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race. The ad was issued amid growing dissatisfaction with the GOP’s handling of key issues among Americans.

In the ad, Obama urged voters, saying, “Mississippi, it’s time for a change. That’s why you need to send Scott Colom to the U.S. Senate.” The message was aimed at encouraging support for Colom’s campaign.
summary: Former President Obama released a new advertisement this week supporting Democratic Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom. The ad urges Mississippians to send Colom to the U. S. Senate amid dissatisfaction with the GOP’s handling of key issues.

title: Flood‑damaged EVs pose fire risk after water recedes, fire officials say
content:
Fire officials say flood‑damaged electric vehicles pose a fire risk even after water recedes.  

Saltwater can damage the lithium‑ion batteries found in electric vehicles, hybrids, electric bicycles and scooters, potentially triggering fires days or even weeks after the initial exposure.
summary: Saltwater can damage lithium‑ion batteries in electric vehicles, hybrids, electric bicycles and scooters. This damage may trigger fires days or weeks after the initial exposure.

content:

content: In a recent court filing, a lawyer representing one of the seven accused Cornell fraternity members has lashing out at Jane Doe’s attorney. title: Delta Postpones Atlanta‑Riyadh Service Until March 2027 After Houthi Attacks
content:
Delta Air Lines announced on Monday that it will postpone the launch of its new flight service from Atlanta to Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The decision follows deadly attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh by Iran‑backed Houthi rebels.  

In a release, Delta cited “evolving developments in the region” as the reason for the delay. The airline said the new service will now be launched in March 2027.
summary: Delta Air Lines has postponed the launch of its Atlanta to Riyadh flight service until March 2027. The delay follows deadly attacks by Iran‑backed Houthi rebels on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

title: Speaker Mike Johnson warns livestreamed Hasan execution could aid terrorist recruitment
content:
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R‑La.) warned that the Pentagon’s plan to livestream the execution of former Army Major Nidal Malik Hasan could serve as a recruiting tool for terrorist groups.  

In an interview, Johnson said, “There are colleagues that have concerns,” indicating that several of his peers share reservations about broadcasting the execution publicly.  

Johnson’s remarks join a growing list of Republicans who have expressed doubts about the public livestream.
summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson said the Pentagon’s plan to livestream the execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan could be used by terrorist groups to recruit more people. He added that there are colleagues that have concerns about broadcasting it publicly.

title: Texas 15th District Offers Insight Into Latino Voting Patterns
content: The 15th Congressional District in Texas stretches from the east of San Antonio down into the Rio Grande Valley. It is a majority‑Latino district that offers insight into the Latino electorate across the state. The district’s demographic makeup provides a useful lens for understanding how Latino voters are influencing political trends in Texas.
summary: The 15th Congressional District extends from east of San Antonio to the Rio Grande Valley. It is a majority-Latino district that provides a window into the Latino vote in Texas.

content:

Shaheen discussed the terms of the diesel agreement and the president’s assertion that the deal would halt energy tensions, noting that the promised ceasefire failed to come into effect.

content:
A motion of no‑confidence in Sinn Féin ministers, including Michelle O’Neill, has been deemed “pointless” by O’Neill.  

The motion will be debated in the Northern Ireland Assembly after it received the backing of unionist parties last week. The motion targets O’Neill and three other Sinn Féin ministers.

content: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has criticized the prime minister, Rishi Sunak, for "unpicking" the trade agreement the United Kingdom signed with the European Union. This statement comes as the prime minister prepares to advocate for new post-Brexit deals at an upcoming EU summit.

title: UN regulator requires cookstove projects to cover risk of tree loss
content:
The United Nations regulator has mandated that cookstove projects must now account for the risk of future forest loss. This new requirement compels these initiatives to protect against the possibility that the trees they save may be destroyed later.

This regulatory change marks the first time such a provision has been implemented for cookstove projects. The decision was made despite lobbying efforts aimed at securing an exemption from these new protections.
summary: The UN regulator has, for the first time, required cookstove projects to cover the risk that the trees they save are later destroyed. This follows lobbying for an exemption.
author: Climate Home News

title: Rescued turtles return to Gingham water hole after NSW government cut flows
content:
Ten broad-shelled turtles and three Murray River turtles have been released back into the Gingham water hole in New South Wales’ Gwydir region. The freshwater turtles were previously rescued from the dried-up water hole after the state government halted environmental water to the area.

The cessation of water flows followed a complaint from a private landholder, an action that reportedly led to the deaths of wildlife and sheep.
summary: Ten broad-shelled turtles and three Murray River turtles were released back into the Gingham water hole in western New South Wales. The turtles had been rescued from the dried-up water hole after the state government halted environmental water to the area following a complaint from a private landholder.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Super El Niño Threatens Food System; Farms Can Prepare
content:
Liz Carlisle, an associate professor of Environmental Studies at UC Santa Barbara, highlights the threat that a potentially record-breaking El Niño poses to the global food system. While forecasters warn that Central and South America, the Caribbean, and southern Africa will face the most severe impacts, Carlisle notes that the United States could still experience significant crop losses due to severe weather.

To mitigate these risks, Carlisle advocates for agricultural practices that protect soil amid potential flooding, such as planting cover crops or perennial plants. She emphasizes that Congress must take action to protect these regenerative farming methods. Carlisle is the author of Healing Grounds: Climate, Justice, and the Deep Roots of Regenerative Farming and co-editor of Living Roots: The Promise of Perennial Foods.
summary: Forecasters warn that this year's El Niño could become the strongest on record, raising concerns about its impact on agriculture and food security. Farmers can protect soil by planting cover crops or perennial plants, but Congress must act to safeguard these practices.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Judge Halts Tree Cutting at East Potomac Golf Course Amid Trump Expansion Plans
content:
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued a 24-hour order on Monday halting tree removal at the historic East Potomac golf course, a site Donald Trump is considering for expansion. The judge granted the temporary stay while she reviews an emergency request from plaintiffs who argue that construction activities are proceeding despite a pending legal challenge.

Reyes stated that the plaintiffs are likely to suffer immediate and irreparable harm without preliminary relief. She specifically noted that tree removal for routine maintenance is not exempt from the order, directing Trump officials to explain the cutting of trees at the location.
summary: US district judge Ana Reyes ordered a 24‑hour halt to tree cutting at the historic East Potomac golf course. The order was issued while Reyes considers an emergency relief request from plaintiffs who say Donald Trump’s expansion plans are proceeding despite a pending lawsuit.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Early gut microbes aid newborn immune system against infections, mouse studies show
content:
New research using mouse experiments indicates that early gut microbes assist the newborn immune system in combating deadly infections. While infants are born with a baseline level of immunity, they possess fewer defensive mechanisms than adults to fight diseases.

The developing immune system relies on exposure to pathogens to build its repertoire, a process that simultaneously leaves babies vulnerable to infection because many immune defenses are still maturing.
summary: Mouse experiments suggest that early gut microbes help the newborn immune system fight deadly infections. Newborns have limited immune tools compared to adults, making them vulnerable to infection despite some innate immunity.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study finds protein linked to Alzheimer's may alter brain immune cell fat handling and inflammation
content:
Researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz and Pacific Northwest National Laboratory have identified a potential mechanism linking a genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease to brain immune cell function. The study suggests that a protein associated with the disease can alter how these immune cells process fat and trigger inflammation.

This finding offers a new clue into why certain individuals are more susceptible to developing Alzheimer's. By modifying the activity of brain immune cells, the protein may help explain how established genetic risks influence brain health and disease progression.
summary: Researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz and Pacific Northwest National Laboratory found a new clue that may help explain why some people are more likely to develop Alzheimer's disease. The clue suggests that a protein linked to the disease can change how the brain's immune cells handle fat and trigger inflammation, potentially
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study links rising brain cancer risk to increased radon exposure
content:
A recent study has linked brain cancer risk to higher levels of radon exposure. The research involved long‑term tracking of nearly 160,000 people from across the United States.

The analysis found that as individuals’ exposure to radon increased, so did their risk of developing brain cancer. The findings suggest a direct correlation between elevated radon concentrations and brain cancer incidence.
summary: Long-term tracking of nearly 160,000 people across the United States suggests that brain cancer risk rises as exposure to radon increases. The findings indicate a connection between elevated concentrations of radon and higher brain cancer risk.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Water Shape at Tau Hotspot Drives Dementia-Linked Clumping
content:
Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia are classified as neurodegenerative tauopathies, conditions in which tau proteins within the brain misfold and result in cognitive decline. The specific mechanism by which misfolded tau recruits other healthy tau proteins to misfold and clump has previously remained unclear.

Recent research indicates that the shape of water at a key tau hotspot plays a role in driving this dementia-linked clumping process.
summary: The study shows that the shape of water at a key tau hotspot helps drive the clumping of tau proteins, which is linked to diseases such as Alzheimer's and frontotemporal dementia. This finding explains how misfolded tau can recruit healthy tau to misfold and aggregate, leading to cognitive decline.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study Finds Long‑Term Alcohol Use and Mental Health Patterns Vary After Disasters
content:
A recent study published in Alcohol: Clinical and Experimental Research examined how exposure to disasters shapes long‑term mental health and alcohol use. Researchers found that individuals who experienced disasters displayed distinct trajectories of alcohol consumption and mental health outcomes that were interrelated.

The analysis revealed that both individual differences and the specific type of disaster influenced these patterns. The findings underscore the persistent mental and behavioral health challenges faced by disaster survivors.

The study highlights the need for interventions that are tailored to each survivor’s mental health profile in order to prevent problem drinking.
summary: The study, published in Alcohol: Clinical and Experimental Research, found that people exposed to disasters show different long‑term patterns of alcohol use and mental health. It highlights the need for interventions tailored to individuals' mental health profiles to prevent problem drinking.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Broad Institute study shows drug combo reducing oxygen improves Parkinson's symptoms in mice
content: Broad Institute researchers have reported that a combination of two small-molecule chemicals that reduce oxygen delivery to cells improved symptoms of neurodegeneration in a mouse model of Parkinson's disease. This new study builds on prior findings by the scientists, who had previously identified that excess oxygen in the brain is associated with neuronal death in Parkinson's disease. Their earlier research also indicated that reducing the oxygen levels inhaled by mice could help reverse disease symptoms.
summary: Broad Institute researchers found that two small-molecule chemicals that reduce oxygen delivery to cells improved symptoms of neurodegeneration in a mouse model of Parkinson's disease. The study builds on earlier findings that excess oxygen in the brain is linked to neuronal death and that reducing the oxygen that mice breathe could help reverse symptoms.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Johns Hopkins Study Links Blood Pressure Protein to Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenia
content:
Johns Hopkins Medicine researchers reported in a preliminary study that a protein involved in blood pressure regulation may serve as a marker for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and other psychoses. The findings suggest the protein could potentially play a role in these conditions.

The study analyzed blood and spinal fluid samples from 200 individuals to investigate this connection.
summary: Johns Hopkins Medicine researchers conducted a preliminary study using blood and spinal fluid samples from 200 people. They found evidence that a protein involved in blood pressure regulation may serve as a marker for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and other psychoses.
author: Medical Xpress

title: FAA warns U.S. airlines of safety risks over Saudi Arabia after attacks
content:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has warned U. S. airlines about safety risks for flights over Saudi Arabia. The warning follows recent attacks on Riyadh airport that have disrupted travel in the region.  

Delta Air Lines is evaluating the possibility of launching a new service on Oct. 23, amid the heightened security concerns.

content:
Delta has postponed the launch of its new service to Saudi Arabia until March following the attacks on Riyadh airport.  

The airline had originally scheduled the route to begin on Oct. 23, a launch that would have marked the first nonstop commercial flight between the United States and Saudi Arabia.

title: Trump’s deal with Putin will have little impact on US diesel prices, experts say
content:
Donald Trump’s agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to temporarily lift U.S. sanctions on imports of Russian diesel is expected to have little “meaningful” effect on motorists and businesses in the United States and abroad, analysts said. The deal, announced on Friday, would allow the United States to import millions of tonnes of diesel, but experts warned that the fuel would take weeks to ship and that the quantity is too small to influence U.S. fuel prices.

Energy and foreign‑policy analysts also noted that the full terms of the agreement are unlikely to be met, citing damage to Russian refineries that would limit production. The agreement was met with criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who called the deal “news to me” and expressed anger at Trump’s announcement.

Trump posted on Truth Social that the diesel supply was essential to reduce fuel prices, which have surged after his decision to go to war against Iran.
summary: Energy and foreign policy analysts say

title: Hall and Woodford Awarded 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics for Crisis‑Smoothing Models
content:
The 2026 Nobel Prize in economics was awarded to two U.S. economists for developing models that help central bankers and finance ministers stabilize their economies.

Robert Hall of Stanford University, California, and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, New York, were recognized for creating the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation.” Their work provides policymakers with tools to smooth out the peaks and troughs of their economies, thereby avoiding long recessions and runaway inflation.
summary: Robert Hall of Stanford University, California, and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, New York, received the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics for developing models that help central bankers and finance ministers stabilise their economies. Their work provides microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation, giving policymakers better tools to smooth out economic peaks and troughs.

content: HMV announced that its Oxford Street store will close after three years of operation. The music retailer said the location is “unviable” and that it is searching for a new site in London’s West End. No further details about the closure or the prospective replacement location were provided.
summary: HMV announced it will close its Oxford Street store, which has been open for three years. The retailer said the site is unviable and it is seeking a new location in London's West End.

title: Escape rooms give health care students a safe place to get things wrong
content: Three occupational therapy students are currently using escape rooms as a learning tool, a method designed to provide a safe environment for them to make mistakes. In one instance, the students believed they had correctly determined the next steps for their patient’s care, but a buzzer signaled that their answer was incorrect.
summary: Three occupational therapy students participated in an escape room exercise. They believed they had determined the correct next step for a patient, but they were wrong.
author: Phys.org

title: Primordial helium confirms Big Bang composition
content:
In the early moments of the Big Bang, hydrogen and helium were the primary elements forged, with the early universe consisting of approximately three parts hydrogen to one part helium. While tiny traces of light elements like lithium were also produced, they were not of significant consequence.

All heavier elements, including the oxygen in human lungs and the iron in blood, were created later through astrophysical processes. These elements were fused in stars, formed in supernovae, or scattered by collisions between neutron stars.

In the present cosmos, heavier elements are so rare that astronomers collectively classify them as metals.
summary: In the early moments of the Big Bang, hydrogen and helium were forged, with a ratio of about three parts hydrogen to one part helium, and tiny traces of lithium were also produced. Heavier elements such as oxygen and iron were later created in stars, supernovae, and neutron star collisions.
author: Phys.org

title: UCLA study links 2024 record rainfall to El Niño and global warming
content:
A new study from UCLA has found that the 2024 El Niño has already set a record for extreme rainfall, with 40 % of the increase linked to global warming. The research notes that strong El Niños have occurred only four times in as many decades, yet the 2024 event is already showing signs of a sequel.

The UCLA team’s analysis indicates that the unprecedented rainfall is tied to the warming climate, and that the current atmospheric conditions are favorable for another intense El Niño. The study highlights that the 2024 event broke the previous record for extreme rainfall associated with El Niño.

These findings suggest that the climate system is primed for a repeat of the 2024 rainfall pattern, underscoring the growing impact of global warming on El Niño events.
summary: UCLA research found that 2024 broke the record for extreme rainfall, with 40% of the increase tied to global warming. The study notes that strong El Niños have occurred only four times in as many decades and that conditions are ripe for a repeat.
author: Phys.org

title: Audit staffing structure improves audit outcomes, study finds
content:
New research from the University at Buffalo School of Management indicates that the staffing structure of an audit office significantly influences audit outcomes. The study highlights the distinct roles within audit firms, where partners oversee audits and client relationships, managers supervise teams and projects, and staff handle much of the day-to-day work.

The findings suggest that audit quality improves when a higher number of audit partners and managers are actively involved in supervising and reviewing audit engagements.
summary: Audit firms use partners, managers, and staff in a tiered structure. Research from the University at Buffalo School of Management shows that greater partner and manager involvement improves audit quality.
author: Phys.org

title: Tiny fossils reveal a missing chapter of ocean life after Snowball Earth
content: A rare collection of micro- and macro-fossils discovered in a roadside outcrop in South China provides insight into marine life following one of Earth's most extreme ice ages. The assemblage includes distinct structures such as thin ribbons, branching shapes, and a tiny balloon on a stalk. These findings offer a glimpse into the biological history of the oceans during this period.
summary: A rare assemblage of micro- and macro-fossils was found in a roadside outcrop in South China. The fossils, which include thin ribbons, branching shapes, and a tiny balloon on a stalk, provide evidence of marine life after the Snowball Earth ice age.
author: Phys.org

title: Neuroscientists and philosophers debate Claude's global workspace on luxury yacht
content:
A debate about artificial intelligence and consciousness recently took place on a luxury yacht. The discussion brought together neuroscientists and philosophers to examine whether the chatbot Claude might exhibit a form of consciousness.

The conversation centered on a leading theory of consciousness that describes experience as information flowing through a global workspace in the mind. Participants explored whether similar patterns could be detected in Claude’s internal processes.

The debate highlighted the possibility that AI systems like Claude might process information in a way that mirrors the global workspace model, raising questions about the emergence of consciousness in artificial agents.
summary: A leading theory of consciousness posits experience as information flowing through a global workspace in the mind. Neuroscientists and philosophers debated signs of a similar workspace in the chatbot Claude while on a luxury yacht.
author: New Scientist

title: Monte Verde controversy reignites debate over first peoples in the Americas
content: The archaeological sites at Monte Verde in Chile continue to spark debate among experts regarding the initial human inhabitants of the Americas. Columnist Michael Marshall reports that this long-standing controversy is intensifying once again, with discussions potentially reshaping the understanding of early migration to the continent.
summary: The Monte Verde sites in Chile have sparked decades of arguments among archaeologists regarding the first inhabitants of the Americas. Columnist Michael Marshall reports that the dispute is intensifying and could alter current understanding of early human presence in the region.
author: New Scientist

title: Russia’s silence on lab worker’s plague death raises pandemic preparedness concerns
content:
Devi Sridhar, a scientist, argues that Russia’s silence regarding the death of a laboratory worker highlights a critical failure in pandemic preparedness, stating that such efforts are ineffective if information about threats is withheld. While scientists typically focus on technical challenges such as identifying pathogens and developing vaccines, Sridhar emphasizes that political factors significantly impact global health security.

The recent incident involving a suspected pneumonic plague case in Russia has generated global headlines, a development Sridhar notes was unpredictable. Although the World Health Organization (WHO) monitors thousands of potential disease signals monthly, the specific circumstances of this case are considered unusual due to the lack of transparency from Russian authorities. Sridhar points to ongoing concerns about biological weapons research as a key factor in the heightened attention surrounding the incident.
summary: Russia has not provided information about the death of a lab worker suspected of having pneumonic plague. The lack of transparency has raised concerns about pandemic preparedness and potential biological weapons research.
author: Guardian Science

title: NASA Sends Health Research to ISS on SpaceX CRS-35 Mission
content:
NASA’s SpaceX CRS‑35 mission will carry a suite of health‑research experiments to the International Space Station. The payload focuses on human and plant health as well as drug‑resistant organisms.

The experiments will be launched aboard SpaceX’s 35th Commercial Resupply Services flight from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The mission is part of NASA’s effort to advance research that benefits life on Earth and supports future exploration.

The research is intended to support astronaut health during long‑duration missions.
summary: NASA experiments on human and plant health and drug-resistant organisms will travel to the International Space Station aboard SpaceX’s 35th Commercial Resupply Services mission from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The research supports astronaut health during long‑duration missions and benefits life on Earth and future exploration.
author: NASA News

content:

content:

content:
A Jacobin article titled “Publishers Killed the Paperback, Then Blamed Readers” has been posted online. The piece can be accessed at https://jacobin.com/2026/10/books-publishing-reading-mass-market-paperback.

content:
Codex CLI installs a persistent, self‑updating background daemon by default
